frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d191:
Acting Secretary of State Edward Stettinius wrote to Wallace Murray, the State Department's adviser on political relations, on 5 November 1943. The short secret note passes on items from that day's meeting with President Roosevelt, some for Murray's information and some needing action.

Roosevelt admits he does not grasp the Middle East oil problem and asks for a two-page brief on it at once. He floats a trusteeship for the region shared by Russia, Britain, and America. He also wants a four-power commission for French West Africa, and he sounds annoyed with de Gaulle. A final item, on Turkey, is marked secret and passed on only in conversation, so its content stays off the page.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d291:
John Martin, Prime Minister Churchill's private secretary, sent a short secret covering note to Harry Hopkins at Cairo on 23 November 1943, enclosing a British telegram from Jedda dated 15 November. Churchill, writing as Colonel Warden, had asked Martin to show Hopkins the telegram and have it returned.

The enclosure reports King Ibn Saud's complaint from Mecca. An American representative in Jedda had put seven pointed questions to him about Saudi arms requests to Britain: what was asked, what was promised, and what had arrived. The king answered that fifty light reconnaissance cars were promised and none had come. The British minister calls the questions unfortunate, since they suggest distrust between the allies, and urges a quick joint agreement on arms for Saudi Arabia.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d391:
Three unrelated reports for the President at Tehran were gathered into a secret telegram Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt from Washington on 29 November 1943. It is a typical Hull digest, moving from China to Portugal in a few lines.

Chungking reports news from a Chinese source who had lately seen Japanese and puppet officials at Nanking. Japan keeps making unsuccessful peace offers to Chiang's government. Former foreign minister Matsuoka left Japan on 7 October. His errand was to try to arrange peace between Germany and the Soviet Union. A consul at Kweilin reports Changteh in flames and Changsha expected to fall with only token defense. Finally, Salazar's speech of 26 November stressed British and American assurances of Portuguese sovereignty over the Azores, and Portuguese press accounts set that American part in italics.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d491:
Madame Chiang Kai-shek wrote to President Roosevelt on December 5, 1943. She had stood beside her husband, Generalissimo Chiang, at the first Cairo Conference in November, serving as his voice in English, and China had won public pledges in the Cairo Declaration. The State Department printed her letter in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Few figures moved between the Chinese and American leadership as Madame Chiang did; she had addressed the United States Congress earlier in 1943. A letter from her to Roosevelt carried the weight of the China theater and of her own standing in Washington. It shows the personal diplomacy that held the Chinese alliance together.
frus-1944-quebec-d91:
Treasury staff prepared a briefing book dated September 9, 1944. Briefing books gather facts and positions for busy leaders. The State Department printed this one in the Quebec 1944 volume. It appeared three days before the conference opened.

A briefing book aims to give one reader everything needed. Treasury officials packed figures and arguments into a single volume. Money questions awaited the leaders at Quebec that month. They included aid to Britain and Germany's economic future. For readers, the book shows how departments arm their chiefs. Pages of staff work stood behind each short summit discussion.
frus-1944-quebec-d191:
Mackenzie King's notes, reprinted by the editors, preserve his conversation with Roosevelt just before dinner at Quebec. King raised Canada's part in the Pacific war. Canada was prepared to fight Japan, he said, but in the northern or central regions. Roosevelt answered that a token representation should suffice, and that nothing might be needed for some time.

The president hinted Canadian men might be useful driving the Japanese from northern China toward the war's end. He also said Canada should have a token force to march into Berlin. On Russia, King asked directly what part Stalin would play against Japan. Roosevelt repeated what had been said earlier and added that Stalin had given his word himself.
frus-1944-quebec-d291:

Churchill arrived a day later with his wife, daughter Mary, and a party including Leathers, Ismay, and Moran, leaving on the night of September 19 for the Queen Mary and England. Guests included the Duke of Windsor at lunch and Morgenthau at dinner.

Because Churchill was a guest in Roosevelt's home, their conversations were informal and unminuted, as was the president's custom. Leahy's account lists the substance. There were political questions on Italy, Yugoslavia, and Russia. There was signature of the Octagon report, and drafting of a statement on Italy. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d91:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson put his views on the peace machinery in writing on 23 January 1945. His memorandum to the Secretary of State is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It lists the points he had tried to make at their meeting the day before.

Stimson recalls that the Moscow Conference of 1943 had in view two bodies. One was a general body open to all peace-loving states, large and small. The other was a stopgap body of the four large powers, to guard security while order was restored. The powers that won the war, he argues, must keep the world safe until a lasting system stands. Their stopgap body should be formal, and hard at work.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d191:
Hold everything on Italy, Stettinius cabled from Caserta on 30 January 1945. His top secret message to Acting Secretary Grew, sent from Allied Force Headquarters in Italy, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It concerns a joint statement he had not yet seen.

The Combined Civil Affairs Committee has prepared a proposed joint statement on Italy. Stettinius hopes Grew will hold up any action on it. He has not seen the text, but the feeling at headquarters is that issuing it in its present form would be most unfortunate. He asks Grew to cable the full text and its status. Thomas Thomson was a working chemist who wrote in the early 1800s, when the science was still young. To answer, he gathers cases of magic, taboo, and dying gods from peoples all over the world. He argues that human thought moved from magic toward religion and then science. tob-0191:

Councils, relics, and the planting of the sacred Bo tree receive careful record. Later chronicles drew on its lists of kings and elders. As the oldest historical record of Buddhism's southern school, the Dipavamsa anchors the island's memory of itself. Verified from the 1919 edition, Oldenberg's version remains the scholar's entry to the chronicle tradition.
stargate-program-summary-1991:
The Defense Intelligence Agency summed up its psychic spy program in a short paper of May 15, 1991. The STAR GATE Program Summary is the program's own official overview, freed for release years later. STAR GATE was the last name of the long remote viewing effort.

The summary tells what the program sought, how its viewers worked, and what its chiefs claimed for it. Viewers were tasked to describe far and hidden targets by mind alone. The paper is brief, dry, and strange in equal parts. It is the first file to read on the whole remote viewing affair.
bierce-tales-of-soldiers-1891:
Civil War tales make up most of Ambrose Bierce's Tales of Soldiers and Civilians, from 1891. Bierce fought in that war and knew its cost first hand. His best known tale traps a man at Owl Creek Bridge at the hour of his death.

Sharp wit cuts through each tale. Ghosts walk, but so do fear, pride, and self lies. Bierce trusts no fine words about war or honor. That pain gives his bleak jokes a weight that mere wit can't match.
judge-letters-that-have-helped-me-1891:
Warm notes from a guide fill Letters That Have Helped Me, William Q. Judge's book of 1891. Judge wrote the notes to Julia Keightley, a keen fan of the creed. She set them in print with his leave, since they had helped her so much on the path.

Each note deals with doubt, grief, pride, or zeal in plain, kind words. There is no grand creed here, just close counsel. Fans call it the warm heart of the creed in the United States. Seekers still turn to it in hard times. Keightley, who got the notes, was a scribe in her own right. Her choice to share them gave the creed a warm, close text.
waite-the-occult-sciences-1891:
A. E. Waite mapped the whole field of lore in The Occult Sciences, his survey of 1891. One book takes in magic, the great art of gold, and the arts that read fate. Waite sorts high creed from low trick. He gives each art its roots, chief books, and claims in brief.

The survey is calm, fair, and plain in speech. New fans could grasp the whole map from it at once. It is Waite's one tome guide to the field. Few guides of its age hold up so well for a first read. Waite knew the bands and book shops of the field at first hand. That range lets him weigh each art with a calm, fair hand.
ochorowicz-mental-suggestion-1891:
Julian Ochorowicz links the trance to thought leaps in Mental Suggestion, his study in English from 1891. Ochorowicz was a sage of Poland who worked in Paris. He found that a mind in deep trance can take a mute bid from a far mind, with no word, sign, or touch to bear the thought from one to the next.

Tests with a young seer fill the book. He prints hits and fails with fair care. His work stands at the join of two fields. It helped turn trance craft to the study of thought leaps.
cattan-geomancie-1591:
Christopher Cattan, a Genevan in French service, wrote this guide to geomancy, the art of telling fate from earth signs. Francis Sparry turned it into English, and it came out in 1591. It was the first full English book on the art.

The guide shows how to cast dots at chance, set them in rows, and read the shapes that form. Each shape has a name and a sense, tied to luck, loss, love, or war. English books on the art for the next age all drew on Cattan's scheme. The text keeps the old terms and charts of the art intact.
prestwich-chalk-plateau-1891:
Joseph Prestwich, a great English rock scholar, staked his name on the Kent flint claims in this paper of 1891. Benjamin Harrison, a Kent shop man, had found rough flints on the chalk hills that he held to be tools. Prestwich backed him in print, with the talk that came next in full.

The flints, called eoliths, were said to show man at work before the ice age in Britain. Prestwich tells of their beds, depth, and worn forms as proof of true tools, not chance stones. The paper is a grand man's bold bet, held in the full record of its day.
hartland-science-fairy-tales-1891:
Edwin Sidney Hartland, an English man of law and lore, wrote this study of fairy tales in 1891. It was one of the first books to treat the tales as a theme for strict study. Hartland held that tales keep the marks of the old ways of the folk.

He traces one tale type, the swan maid, through land after land and age after age. The Melusine tale, the fairy bride who is part snake, stands at the heart of his case. The book shows how one tale can map the spread of lore round the world.
wilde-house-pomegranates-1891:
Oscar Wilde wrote these four tales for grown readers, and the set came out in 1891. Its name plays on the rich red fruit of the pomegranate tree. Wilde was then at the height of his fame in the London world of art.

Among the tales stands 'The Fisherman and his Soul,' a long tale of a man and a mermaid. He cuts his soul from his body to wed the maid of the sea, and pays a high price. The set shows Wilde's tale craft at its most rich and grave.
dorian-gray-1891:
Oscar Wilde's sole novel came out in book form in 1891, grown from the magazine text of the year past. He added new parts and a famed preface of sharp, bright lines on art. The book is the form in which most readers have met Dorian Gray since.

Dorian sells his soul, in effect, for youth that does not fade with the years. The portrait in his loft bears the marks of age and sin while he stays fair and young. The tale is the dark crown of the art for art's sake creed of its age.
leland-gypsy-sorcery-1891:
Charles Godfrey Leland wrote on the lore of the Romani folk for years. His Gypsy Sorcery and Fortune Telling came out in 1891. The book gathers charms, spells, and ways to read fate. Much of it came from Romani men and women he knew in England.

Love charms, cures, and signs for luck fill the pages in strong runs. Leland gives the words of the spells and the acts that go with them. He also tells of gods and fays the folk held dear. The book is a rich store of folk magic from its age.
ripley-compound-of-alchymy-1591:
George Ripley was an English canon and alchemist of the 1400s. His Compound of Alchymy is a poem in twelve gates. The print here is the 1591 dress of the work. It is the chief poem of English alchemy.

Each gate is a step in the Great Work, from first rot to the red stone. Ripley veils his craft in rich signs: kings, beasts, and baths of dew. He warns the false hand and cheers the true son of the art. The poem's fame kept it in print for two hundred years.
sbe-32-vedic-hymns-1-1891:
F. Max Muller gave the Vedic Hymns, Part One, English dress in 1891. The work is Book Thirty-Two of the Sacred Books of the East. The hymns come from the Rig Veda, the most old text of India. Muller spent his life on the Vedas at Oxford.

The hymns here praise the Maruts, the storm gods who ride with Rudra. Rudra, Vayu, and Vata get hymns of their own in the set. Wild winds, rain, and the crash of the storm fill the old songs. Muller's notes weigh each hard word and old rite in the text.
sbe-40-taoist-texts-2-1891:
James Legge gave the Texts of Taoism English dress in the Sacred Books of the East. Book Forty, from 1891, is Part Two of that work. It holds the last books of the Writings of Kwang-dze, known now as Zhuangzi. Zhuangzi is the great wit and sage of the Taoist line.

Books Eighteen to Thirty-Three close the vast, wild text here. Tales of a butterfly dream, a huge fish, and free roams of the mind fill the pages. Zhuangzi mocks stiff rites and the praise of the crowd. Legge's dress was the first full one of the work in English.
ariosto-orlando-furioso-harington-1591:
Ludovico Ariosto wrote Orlando Furioso in Italian in the early 1500s. Sir John Harington gave it English dress in 1591, the first full one in the tongue. Harington was a court wit at the court of Queen Elizabeth. The poem is a vast tale of knights, love, and war.

Orlando goes mad for love of Angelica, who loves him not. Knights ride to the Moon to fetch back his lost wits in a vial. Saracen wars, spells, and strange beasts crowd the long, bright tale. Harington's verse keeps the fun and verve of the source in full.
ibsen-hedda-gabler-archer-1891:
Henrik Ibsen wrote Hedda Gabler in Norwegian, and William Archer made this English version in 1891. Archer, the critic who brought Ibsen to England, knew the playwright's aims at first hand. Hedda is often called his most dangerous heroine, a caged mind with pistols and pride.

Hedda, wed to the dull scholar Tesman, is bored, pregnant, and trapped in respectability. Her old flame Lövborg returns with a great book and a wild past of drink. Hedda burns his manuscript, lends him a pistol, and is trapped by Judge Brack's knowledge. She shoots herself rather than live under scandal and another man's power over her life. The play's cold grip and Hedda's mystery keep stages busy to this day.
gissing-new-grub-street-1891:
George Gissing published New Grub Street in 1891, his definitive novel of the writing life in London. Hack writers starve while mediocrities prosper, in the bitterest portrait of literary trade written. Gissing, who had starved, knew every rung of the ladder they climb and fall in London.

Edwin Reardon, a novelist of talent, cannot write the three-volume potboilers the market demands and sinks toward death in poverty. Jasper Milvain, his friend, treats literature as a trade, charms editors and widows, and rises by knowing the business of books. Amy, Reardon's wife, leaves him for failure and in time weds the rising Milvain, in Gissing's coldest turn of the screw. The title names the old Grub Street of hired pens, reborn in the magazine age. The book remains the set text for every writer who has feared the market's verdict.
lagerlof-gosta-berling-1891:
Selma Lagerlof published The Story of Gosta Berling in 1891, her first novel, set in Varmland in Sweden. Gosta Berling is a priest removed from his post for drinking. He joins a band of retired officers and idlers at Ekeby Manor. Their year of feasts, pranks, and loves drives the tale.

Legends, ghosts, and folk tales weave through the main story. The lady of the manor holds the cavaliers in check until a dark bargain unsettles all. Lagerlof writes in a rich, song-like style. The book made her famous at home and abroad. She later became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
hardy-tess-1891:
Thomas Hardy published Tess of the d'Urbervilles in 1891, a novel about a poor country girl in Wessex. Tess Durbeyfield learns her family claims kinship with an old noble line. Sent to claim kin, she meets Alec d'Urberville, who ruins her. She later finds love with Angel Clare, a parson's son learning farming.

Tess tells Angel her past on their wedding night, and he cannot forgive her. Hard work, desertion, and want follow before a final, fatal reunion. Hardy subtitled the book the story of a pure woman. Its attack on double standards shocked Victorian readers. It remains his most loved and argued-over novel.
browne-travellers-narrative-1891:
Browne's Traveller's Narrative, published in 1891, translates a Persian history of the Babi movement written to explain the episode of the Bab. The Bab was the young Persian prophet executed in 1850 whose claims split his country. Browne added a long introduction and notes of his own.

The narrative tells of the Bab's preaching, the sieges of his followers, and the faith that grew from the ruins. Browne prints the account as his Persian author gave it, letting an insider's voice carry the story. The book became the foundational Western source on the Bab and the origins of the Baha'i faith.
saussaye-manual-science-religion-1891:
Pieter Daniel Chantepie de la Saussaye was an Amsterdam professor whose Manual of the Science of Religion, in this 1891 English edition, helped name a field. The science of religion was then new, split between history and philosophy. His manual gave it a method and a map.

De la Saussaye sets out phenomenology, the ordered description of rites, myths, and ideas, before judging any of them. He treats prayer, sacrifice, priesthood, and sacred books as forms that recur across the world. Textbook writers across Europe built on his scheme, and his terms still echo in the field.
russell-studies-scriptures-vol3-1891:
Russell's Thy Kingdom Come, published in 1891, is volume three of Studies in the Scriptures. The book turns from chronology to the papacy, prophecy, and the coming kingdom itself. Russell's followers read it as the sequel that showed what the dates would bring.

He reads the book of Revelation and the parables as a coded history of the church age ending in harvest. The great pyramid of Egypt even enters his argument as a stone witness to the divine plan. The volume deepened the movement's sense of living at the turn of the ages. Russell treats prophecy as a timetable that careful Bible study can read.
newes-from-scotland-1591:
Newes from Scotland appeared in 1591, a pamphlet reporting the North Berwick witch trials in Scotland. The accused, including schoolmaster John Fian, were charged with raising storms against King James VI at sea. Torture produced confessions, and the pamphlet spread the story in England.

Pages describe meetings with the Devil, charms, and plots against the king's ships, as the court claimed they happened. James himself took part in questioning the accused, and his interest shaped the case. The pamphlet is a primary source for a famous witch trial. It also shows how print turned a local panic into national news.
guaita-serpent-de-la-genese-1891:
Stanislas de Guaita published Le Serpent de la Genèse in 1891, the first part of a planned large work on evil and the occult. De Guaita was a French poet and Martinist who helped revive occult study in Paris. He read the Bible's serpent as a key to a hidden tradition.

Through Genesis and later lore, de Guaita traced the serpent as a symbol of secret knowledge, temptation, and hidden powers. He drew on Kabbalah, old grimoires, and tales of sorcery and poison. The work is dense, learned, and openly on the side of the occult against a purely material age. It shows French occultism at its most literary and ambitious.
boswell-life-of-johnson-vol1-1791:
James Boswell was a young Scottish lawyer who attached himself to Samuel Johnson, the most famous English writer of the age. For over twenty years Boswell kept notes of their talks. His Life of Samuel Johnson appeared in 1791, and this is its first volume.

Boswell follows Johnson from his poor early years through his dictionary work and rising fame in London. The real glory of the book is the conversation: arguments, jokes, and bold opinions recorded almost word for word. Readers meet a whole circle of writers and wits. It is often called the greatest biography in English.
boswell-life-of-johnson-vol2-1791:
James Boswell spent two decades recording Samuel Johnson's talk, then shaped his notes into a Life published in 1791. This second volume covers Johnson's later years, from the height of his fame to his death.

Johnson dines with the Literary Club, argues with rivals, and tours Scotland with Boswell in the Hebrides journey. Boswell also shows the old man's fears, kindness, and failing health with unusual honesty. Johnson's sharp sayings fill these pages, but so do his friendships and his deep fear of death. The closing chapters record Johnson's last illness and death in 1784. Together the two volumes set the standard for modern biography, and writers still study Boswell's method today.
burns-tam-o-shanter-1791:
Robert Burns wrote Tam o' Shanter in 1790 for a book about Scottish antiquities, and it appeared in print in 1791. Burns was by then a farmer and excise officer living in Dumfriesshire. The poem is a long comic tale in Scots verse.

Tam rides home drunk from the pub on a stormy night and stops to watch witches dancing in a ruined churchyard. The witches spot him and give chase, and his horse barely escapes across a bridge stream. Burns tells the story with speed, warmth, and mock warning about drink. Many readers rank it as the finest work he ever wrote.
tao-te-ching-legge-1891:
James Legge published his complete translation of the Tao Teh King in 1891, as part one of The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East thirty-nine. The Tao Te Ching, ascribed to Lao Tzu, holds eighty-one short chapters of verse-like counsel. It is the founding book of Taoism and one of the most translated texts on earth.

The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao, the book begins, then teaches rule by softness and non-action. Legge adds his introduction and notes, weighing the text's age and meaning with care. His rendering favored exact study over poetic dress. Generations of English students of Chinese thought began with Legge's Lao Tzu. The little book still rewards slow reading.
pearson-fragments-zeno-cleanthes-1891:
Zeno of Citium founded the Stoic school at Athens around 300 BCE, and Cleanthes, his pupil, led it after him. The books of both men are lost. A. C. Pearson gathered what later writers quoted from them, and Cambridge University Press published his English collection in 1891, with an introduction and notes.

Each fragment comes with remarks that explain hard terms and point to the source that kept the words alive. Through these scraps readers can trace early Stoic teaching on fate, nature, and virtue. Pearson's book was the first English gathering of the pair. It still serves as a direct door into the first age of the Stoa.
herbart-textbook-psychology-1891:
Johann Friedrich Herbart wrote his Lehrbuch zur Psychologie, Textbook of Psychology, in 1816, and Margaret K Smith translated it in 1891. Herbart, who held Kant's old chair, treated psychology as a science of the soul's mechanics. Ideas, in his picture, press, check, and lift each other like forces in a crowded field.

From that mechanics Herbart builds his accounts of perception, memory, feeling, and desire. The textbook is spare and ordered, meant to ground his famous pedagogy in the mind's real workings. His Science of Education grows straight from this root, as the evidence of the two books shows. Smith's English carried the system to American students of the mind.
schiller-riddles-sphinx-1891:
Writing under the name A. Troglodyte, F. C. S. Schiller issued Riddles of the Sphinx in 1891. The subtitle calls the work a study in the philosophy of evolution. Schiller was a young Oxford thinker at the time. His book fired an early shot in a long campaign.

The riddles are the old puzzles of life: mind, matter, God, and human worth after Darwin. Schiller argues that thought must start from human needs and acts, not from cold abstraction. That stance grew into his humanist form of pragmatism. The book stands as the founding statement of that program. Its bold tone still startles.
schopenhauer-fourfold-root-1891:
Arthur Schopenhauer wrote On the Fourfold Root as his doctoral dissertation in 1813. Mme. Karl Hillebrand translated the German essay into English in 1891. Its subject is the principle of sufficient reason, the rule that everything has a ground. Schopenhauer claimed the rule takes four distinct forms.

He sorts those forms by the kinds of objects minds can know. Causes in nature, grounds of judgment, and motives for action each follow their own version. Sorting them clears up, he thought, much muddle in older philosophy. The essay lays the base for his whole later system. Readers often start his work here.
lobachevsky-theory-parallels-halsted-189:
Nicholas Lobachevsky broke Euclid's hold on geometry in his Geometrical Researches on the Theory of Parallels. George Bruce Halsted translated the work, first published in German in 1840, into English in 1891. For two thousand years, Euclid's parallel postulate had seemed beyond doubt. Lobachevsky denied it and built a new geometry on the denial.

In his system, many lines through a point can miss a given line entirely. Angles and areas then obey rules strange to school geometry. He shows the system hangs together without contradiction. The book founded non-Euclidean geometry as a field. Later physics found his strange space at work in the real world.
bentham-fragment-government-1891:
Jeremy Bentham fired his first shot in A Fragment on Government in 1776. F. C. Montague edited the text for the 1891 edition held here. Bentham attacked the famed legal writer Blackstone and his praise of English law as it stood. In place of custom and reverence, Bentham demands utility as the test.

Laws should be judged by the happiness they produce, he argues, and by nothing else. That demand founded legal positivism, the study of law as it is, apart from morals. It also launched utilitarian jurisprudence, Bentham's science of law making. The Fragment's preface alone became a classic. Readers meet a young reformer in full cry.
russell-thy-kingdom-come-1891:
Charles Taze Russell issued Thy Kingdom Come in 1891 as the third volume of Millennial Dawn. The series, also called Studies in the Scriptures, set out his reading of prophecy. Bible Students, his movement, awaited Christ's kingdom on a dated scheme. This volume carries that scheme toward its climax.

Its Great Pyramid chapters made pyramidology a doctrine of the movement. Russell read the pyramid's passages as a stone calendar of sacred history. Measurements in inches became years in his prophetic sums. The book is a document of record for the Bible Student faith. It is preserved as history, not as endorsement. Its influence built a lasting movement.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol10-1891:
The tenth and last volume of the Guiding Symptoms closed the set in 1891, eleven years after Hering's death. A project begun from one man's proving notebooks had grown into the largest symptom record of its school. Volume X completes the alphabetical run of remedies.

Its pages follow the house style: symptoms by region, ranks marked, characteristic signs lifted clear. With the set whole, a prescriber could trace almost any proved sign to its remedy. Later abridgments drew heavily on these volumes, yet the full ten still reward anyone who wants Hering in his own fullness.
browne-travellers-narrative-bab-1891:
E. G. Browne gave English readers their first deep look at the Babi movement in A Traveller's Narrative, printed at Cambridge in 1891. The narrative, attributed to 'Abdu'l-Baha, recounts the episode of the Bab, the young prophet executed in Persia in 1850. Browne translated the text and wrapped it in his own introduction and notes.

Persecution, prison, and the split of a new faith fill the account, told by a believer close to its center. Western scholars built their picture of Babism on Browne's edition for years. It remains the primary English witness to the events of 1844 to 1850.
eddy-retrospection-introspection-1891:
Mary Baker Eddy told her own story in Retrospection and Introspection, published in 1891 when her movement was already famous. The short book traces her path from a sickly New England childhood to the discovery she named Christian Science. She recounts her healing, her break with the healer Quimby, and the founding of her church and college.

Eddy writes to fix the record as she wished it kept, answering rivals in her own calm, firm voice. Readers meet the founder not through followers or foes, but through her chosen account of herself and her work. The memoir remains a first source for the movement's beginnings and for Eddy's mind.
codrington-the-melanesians-1891:
Robert Henry Codrington gave the study of religion the word mana in The Melanesians, published in 1891 after long Pacific service. Codrington, a missionary-scholar in the Banks Islands and the Solomons, described the unseen power behind magic, luck, and success. Secret societies, ghosts, stones with power, and the spirits of the dead fill his studies in Melanesian life and folklore.

Mana entered the world's vocabulary from these pages and never left it, spreading into every tongue. Codrington wrote from long residence and real command of local languages, correcting travelers' tales as he went with care. His book founded the serious study of Melanesian religion and remains a delight to read today.
mooney-the-sacred-formulas-of-the-cherok:
James Mooney worked for the Bureau of American Ethnology and lived among the Cherokee, learning their language and gaining their trust. His 1891 report prints the sacred formulas that Cherokee shamans dictated to him, given in Cherokee with English translation.

The formulas are spoken cures and charms: words for healing sickness, for success in hunting and fishing, for war, and for winning love. Each text shows how the shaman named the disease spirit and called on stronger powers against it. Mooney added notes on herbs, rites, and the shamans' own explanations. Few early records preserve native ritual language this fully.
westermarck-the-history-of-human-marriag:
Edward Westermarck, a Finnish scholar working in England, published this Darwinian history of marriage in 1891. It was a large claim for its time: that marriage and the family rest on instincts shaped by natural selection, not on late invention.

Westermarck argues against the idea that early humans lived without marriage rules. He examines exogamy and the incest taboo, proposing that children raised together lose desire for each other, a claim still debated as the Westermarck effect. His evidence spans animals, early peoples, and civilized law. The book became a standard reference in the study of the family.
bartlett-familiar-quotations-1891:
John Bartlett, a Cambridge bookseller, first published Familiar Quotations in 1855 to answer customers who asked where lines came from. The ninth edition of 1891 is the mature Victorian form. It traces famous passages, phrases, and proverbs to their sources.

Quotations run from the Bible and Shakespeare to the poets and statesmen of Bartlett's own day. Full indexes of authors and subjects help readers find a half-remembered line. Bartlett's became the name of the whole genre in America. The 1891 edition shows what the educated world of that age knew by heart, or wished it did. Bartlett himself checked each line against its source with bookseller's care.
plos-pone-0003391:
Petric Kuballa and co-authors studied a gene variant tied to Crohn's disease in this 2008 paper. Crohn's is a painful, long-term inflammation of the gut. Large gene scans had pointed to a variant in a gene called ATG16L1. That gene helps cells clean up and digest their own waste, a process called autophagy.

The team tested how cells with the variant handle a germ that lives inside cells. Cleanup of the invader was impaired in those cells. Poor cleanup may let gut microbes linger and drive inflammation. The finding gives Crohn's research a clear process to target.
plos-pone-0003491:
Nandi Siegfried and co-authors compared trial quality across continents in this 2008 paper. Good trials need fair random assignment and hidden allocation of treatments. Those steps keep bias out of results. No earlier work had focused on HIV/AIDS trials or African trials.

The team checked how trials reported random generation and allocation concealment. African HIV trials reported these steps adequately more often than North American ones. The verdict runs against common assumptions about research standards. It credits African trial teams for rigor often overlooked. Trial quality sets how much trust any drug result deserves at all.
plos-pone-0003591:

The team showed genetically based odor signatures persist despite dietary variation. Changing food did not erase the inherited signature. Individual recognition by smell is thus written into DNA. plos-pone-0003691:

The authors ran a meta-analysis of all candidate gene studies of these conditions in adults. Pooling the data gave firmer ground for judging which gene variants truly raise risk. The combined picture helps doctors and researchers sort real genetic signals from noise in a deadly set of diseases.
plos-pone-0003791:

Disrupting Nrf2 weakened the atherosclerosis that ApoE loss normally causes. The result is counterintuitive: removing an antioxidant master switch slowed plaque. It shows oxidative stress pathways pulling double duty in heart disease, not simple protection. Mouse work of this kind often reframes human disease hunts.
plos-pone-0003891:

Industry and social change keep bringing microbes into contact with new hosts. Those contacts let both sides adapt fast, and new diseases can arise.

The authors set out a metasystem built from simple model organisms. Using several paired models lets labs watch adaptation as it emerges. That view is hard to get from a single host and microbe pair. The frame can help scientists foresee how new host-microbe pairs settle or turn harmful.
plos-pone-0003991:
Lisa M. Mullen, Janine T. Bossé, Sean P. Nair, and co-authors studied a bacterial protein with two talents in 2008. A protein in Pasteurella multocida had been shown to bind fibronectin. Fibronectin binding helps bacteria stick to host tissues. The protein also resembles DNA uptake proteins of competent bacteria.

Their PLOS ONE article covers the ComE1 family across the Pasteurellaceae. Family members combine adhesion and DNA binding traits in one design. One protein doing both jobs may aid survival in host airways. The work widens what competence proteins are thought to do. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004091:
Lee Smith, John Willan, Nick Warr, and co-authors removed a candidate sex gene in mice in 2008. The early gonad can become a testis or an ovary. Chromosomal sex normally decides which path it takes. The team had screened for new genes steering that choice.

Their PLOS ONE article reports the Maestro gene is not required. Mice lacking it showed normal sexual development and fertility. A clear negative narrows the search for true sex-determining factors. It also shows why each candidate needs a knockout test. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004191:
Anna Sawka and colleagues published this interview study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Radioactive iodine treatment, called RAI for short, is often considered after surgery for well-differentiated thyroid cancer. Numbers alone cannot say what that diagnosis and treatment feel like to live through.

The researchers interviewed thyroid cancer survivors about being diagnosed, about the iodine treatment, and about how choices were made. Their accounts show the uncertainty and isolation that the treatment can bring. The study gives clinicians a patient's-eye view to weigh alongside survival statistics when advising on this treatment.
plos-pone-0004291:
Rebecca Mercer and Rachel Wevrick published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. MAGEL2 is one of several genes typically inactivated in Prader-Willi syndrome, a developmental disorder marked by obesity. What the loss of MAGEL2 alone does, without the other syndrome genes, was not well understood.

The team studied mice with a targeted mutation of Magel2. They report that loss of Magel2 impairs reproductive function in these mice. Separating one gene's effects from the full syndrome helps doctors understand which features come from which gene. The syndrome takes its features from several genes lost together.
plos-pone-0004391:
Glowing tags let biologists watch living cells from the inside. Simone Kredel, Franz Oswald, Karin Nienhaus, and co-authors built a new red tag in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper describes mRuby, a single-unit red fluorescent protein. It comes from a variant of the protein eqFP611. The tag is meant for labeling parts inside cells.

mRuby takes in light at 558 nanometers and gives it back at 605. That 47-nanometer gap, called the Stokes shift, is large. A wide gap makes the glow easier to separate from the light used to excite it. The authors report the protein is bright and works as one unit. Those traits suit it for clear imaging of cell structures.
plos-pone-0004491: In 2009, Miracle, Denslow, and Kroll found brain-injury markers in salmon. Spillway-induced head injury in young salmon generated brain II spectrin breakdown products. The fish biomarker flagged dam trauma fast. The finding aids salmon conservation work. The markers mirror human ones closely.
plos-pone-0004591: In 2009, Milner, Harris, and Lockley found a giant resting like a bird. A bird-like resting trace from an Early Jurassic theropod revealed posture and behavior. The crouching dinosaur sat bird-style. The finding links dinosaurs to birds. The tracks were rare.
plos-pone-0004691: In 2009, Pagès, Peyrefitte, and Toung Mve named the mosquito behind grim Gabon's chikungunya. Aedes albopictus was the main vector of the chikungunya outbreak in Gabon. The striped tiger mosquito was trapped. The finding informs vector control efforts. The big outbreak was 2007.
plos-pone-0004791: In 2009, Martínez-Mekler, Alvarez Martínez, and Beltrán found one pattern ruling rankings everywhere anew. cowper-homer-odyssey-1791:
Homer's Odyssey tells of Odysseus, called Ulysses here, and his long trip home after Troy fell. William Cowper turned the Greek epic into English blank verse, and his version came out in 1791. The title page of this edition names him plainly as translator, writing for J. M. Dent and Dutton.

Book one opens with the gods debating the hero's fate while his son Telemachus faces rude suitors at home. Cowper refused the rhyming couplets that Pope had made famous, aiming for a plainer sound closer to the Greek. Monsters, gods, and shipwrecks thus reached common readers in clear and direct English.
cowper-homer-iliad-1791:
Cowper's Iliad, printed in English blank verse in 1791, renders Homer's epic of the Trojan War. The story centers on the rage of Achilles in the last weeks of the long siege of Troy. An edition note shows Cowper revising his own work with care soon after it first appeared.

Readers follow fierce battles, Hector's sad farewell to his family, and the fall of heroes on both sides. Like his Odyssey, this version drops Pope's polished rhymes for a plainer line that tracks the Greek more closely. It was a bold bid against the most famous English Homer of the century, and scholars still weigh it.
garland-main-travelled-roads-1891:
Hamlin Garland's Main-Travelled Roads made his name when it appeared in 1891. Harper's later lists group it with Prairie Folks, Rose of Dutcher's Coolly, and The Eagle's Heart. A note from Garland dated March 1, 1922, fronts this printing.

The tales show farm life in the Middle West with no trace of romance. Mortgaged farms, brutal winters, worn-out women, and the slow crush of debt fill the pages. Under the Lion's Paw stands out as the most cutting farm story in American writing. Readers who hoped for cheerful pioneer tales got a shock, and a new realism in fiction was born.
zola-money-1891:
Caxton issued Money at London in 1900, in Vizetelly's English version. Chapter heads run from The Temple of Mammon through Dreams and Schemes. Saccard Makes a Start and The Bank Is Founded follow in order.

Aristide Saccard returns, and this time his weapon is the stock market itself. His Universal Bank turns into a machine for breeding greed in all Paris. Fortunes rise in a morning and vanish by nightfall in the frenzy. A frontispiece shows the ruined Mazaud with a bullet through his head. Furious and prophetic, the 1891 novel reads like later headlines written a full century early.
guaita-essais-sciences-maudites-2-1891:
Stanislas de Guaita reads the Fall through Kabbalah in Le serpent de la Genese, first part, from 1891. The work forms the first part of the second series of his Essais de sciences maudites. De Guaita led the French occult revival with aristocratic learning and total conviction in magic as a hidden science of the soul.

The serpent of Genesis becomes, in his hands, a key to cosmic law. Hebrew letters, myths, and rites are weighed page by page here. He writes for initiates, dense with symbol and reference throughout. The book shows Paris occultism at its most erudite in the eighteen nineties, a world of salons, orders, and secret doctrine.
guaita-temple-de-satan-1891:
De Guaita launches his Essais de sciences maudites with Le Temple de Satan, in French from 1891. The volume defends esoteric Christianity against two foes at once. Material science on one side and black magic on the other both draw his elegant, scornful fire in this cornerstone of the French occult revival.

He presents magic as a sacred science with strict moral law. Satan's temple, in his telling, is error built into a system. Parisian occultists took the book as a manifesto of their cause. It stands at the head of his life's work, the portal through which readers enter his grand design of essays.
liebeault-therapeutique-suggestive-1891:
Liebault puts suggestion to work in Therapeutique suggestive, in French from 1891, the clinical companion to his book on induced sleep. Case after case shows words curing the so-called incurable at Nancy. Pain, palsy, and nervous ills yield, in his reports, to calm speech and firm expectation in the waking and sleeping states alike.

He records failures beside successes with a practitioner's honesty throughout. The method asks for no drugs, no passes, no stage tricks at all. Colleagues came from abroad to watch the old doctor work. The book forms the practical birth record of the talking cure, a quiet landmark on the road to modern psychotherapy.
walker-pronouncing-1791:
John Walker published his Critical Pronouncing Dictionary in 1791, setting out how English words ought to sound. Walker, once an actor, had become the leading teacher of elocution in London. His book marked the sounds of tens of thousands of words so that any reader could aim at approved speech.

Each entry gives spelling, pronunciation, and meaning, with rules and remarks where usage was in dispute. The dictionary served strivers who knew that accent could open or close doors in British society. For a century it was the authority on respectable pronunciation on both sides of the Atlantic. Its influence lingered in schools and pulpits long after newer guides appeared.
bohm-bawerk-positive-theory-capital-1891:
William Smart translated Bohm-Bawerk's Positive Theory of Capital into English in 1891. The Austrian economist had published the German work in 1889 as his own answer to the questions Marx raised. Where his book on Marx attacked, this one builds: it sets out the Austrian theory of capital and interest in full.

Bohm-Bawerk argues that interest arises because people value present goods more than the same goods in the future. Capital, on his account, is stored-up time: roundabout methods take longer but produce more. He works through wages, profit, and the length of production with great care. The book became the foundation of later theories of interest and a pillar of the Austrian school, shaping economics well into the next century.
husserl-philosophie-der-arithmetik-1891:
Husserl's Philosophy of Arithmetic, published in German in 1891, was his first book. He had trained as a mathematician in Vienna and Berlin, then turned to philosophy under Franz Brentano. The young scholar asked a deceptively plain question: how does the mind grasp number?

The book studies counting, collecting, and the signs we use for numbers, trying to ground arithmetic in acts of the mind. Its method leans on psychology, the very approach Husserl would attack nine years later in the Logical Investigations. A sharp review by Gottlob Frege helped push him toward that change. The debut already shows his care for exact description, straining against the limits of his teachers' psychology. It is the starting point of the long road to phenomenology.
french-constitution-1791:
France adopted its first written constitution in September 1791, the work of the National Constituent Assembly. The Revolution had begun in hope two years before, and the Assembly tried to settle it into ordered liberty. The result was a constitutional monarchy: a king kept on his throne, ruling beside an elected Legislative Assembly.

The charter divides power, promises equality before the law, and guards property and speech, while limiting the vote to men who paid set taxes. The king accepted it under pressure after his failed flight to Varennes. War and radical anger swept the settlement away within a year, and the monarchy fell in 1792. The constitution remains the charter of the Revolution's hopeful phase, liberty under law before the Terror. It also records what the men of 1789 thought a free state should be.
polish-constitution-3-may-1791:
The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth adopted its constitution on 3 May 1791, the first written national constitution in Europe. Reformers in the Great Sejm pushed it through as the Commonwealth weakened and its neighbors circled. The charter was a rescue attempt: strengthen the state before Russia and Prussia could finish dividing it.

The text ends the nobles' right to block all business with a single veto, makes the monarchy hereditary, and gives towns a voice in the state. Catholic faith is kept, with toleration promised to others. Russia answered with invasion, and the partitions wiped Poland from the map within four years. The charter of a nation's last hope, adopted too late, is still honored in Poland's national day.

The paper weighs Mobutu's grip, his rivals, and the price of his friendship. Congo's size and minerals made its politics a Cold War concern far beyond Africa. Analysts had to judge a strongman whose rule would last three decades. The file captures that judgment early, when Mobutu's long reign was still new and untested.
cia-0000009591:

plos-pone-0005491: Parkinson's toxins kill dopamine neurons via powerhouses, and GSK-3-beta is involved. Petit-Paitel and team traced cytosolic and powerhouse GSK-3-beta in MPTP-treated neuronal death. The kinase links energy failure to cell loss. plos-pone-0005591: Low fertility and testicular cancer may share roots. Peng and team fully went over the evidence on their tie. The mix explains a fought link. Breeding health's tied risks, fully tested, ill tracking for men's health, with a meta-number verdict on a touchy question.

The cost-effectiveness analysis guides program design. Paying for follow-through in South Africa, health economics of cancer prevention, with home visits showing measurable returns.

DNA-binding domains' family tree, from genomes, ARF, ABI3, HSI, RAV, and REM united, complete genomes enabling family tree, plant genes.
