plos-pone-0006491: Kidney filter cells run on actin webs. Nabet and team mapped actin-linked protein nets in kidney podocytes via shared RNAs. The filter's frame, charted — tiny filters' framework, decoded, with foot processes. Highly special cells, mRNA co-cleanup: likely network, in two-sided cells.
plos-pone-0006591: A brain receptor boosts a neuron saver. Battaglia and team found mGlu3 switch-on lifts GDNF in striatum neurons. The glutamate dial feeds protection — Parkinson's hopeful path, mapped, in lab parkinsonism. Slow targets, ligands weighed: fewer side effects, striatum in focus.
plos-pone-0009391: Proteins with wildly different building sequences can still fold into the same overall shape — but what holds that shape together? Surveying the entire catalog of known protein folds, these researchers map the web of atom-level contacts inside each fold's core. They find shared interaction networks hiding beneath the sequence differences, a discovery that could sharpen protein design and our grasp of how folds evolved.
plos-pone-0009491: HIV cripples the immune system partly by sabotaging the cells that present targets to defender T cells. This study finds that in monocytes, one key presentation pathway — MHC class II processing — still works in infected people. The preserved function is a hopeful sign: part of the immune machinery survives HIV, and therapies could build on what's left.
plos-pone-0009591: We are all mosaics: chromosome gains and losses in the early embryo leave lasting patchworks in our tissues. This single-cell study of human tissues traces that mosaicism to early instability. The paper reveals that the genome's copy-number variation begins before birth — reshaping how we think about genetic disease.
plos-pone-0010391: Formalin, the classic preservative, makes tissue samples glow under the microscope — and this study turns that quirk into a tool. The fluorescence highlights cell shapes in 3D. The paper offers a simple trick for seeing tissue architecture more clearly. The method needs no special dyes, making 3D cell mapping cheaper and easier.
plos-pone-0010491: Proteins move as hinged parts, not rigid blocks. This study develops a method to identify semi-rigid domains from molecular dynamics simulations. The paper offers a tool for reading protein motion. The method turns raw simulation into moving-part diagrams.
plos-pone-0010591: It sounds backwards: giving diabetes-prone mice a skin allergy protected them. Repeated doses of a contact allergen, causing mild rashes, kept the mice diabetes-free. The immune distraction seems to spare the pancreas. The paper suggests misdirecting immunity could become a therapy.
plos-pone-0010691: Breast tissue grows as branching ducts — guided by sugar chains. This study shows losing the enzyme Ndst1 in mammary cells blocks lobuloalveolar development in mice. The paper reveals a sugar code for organ building. The finding links chemistry to anatomy.
plos-pone-0010791: The Adriatic Sea's underwater weed forests are thinning. This study tests what keeps these sea forests tough — and what breaks them. The paper measures loss and bounce-back. The findings guide repair of vanishing marine habitats. The science defends the sea's green lungs.
plos-pone-0010891: After surgery, pain should fade — but sometimes it stays. This study implicates endocannabinoids, astrocytes, and p38 phosphorylation in pain resolution. The paper maps the recovery pathway. The finding suggests ways to prevent chronic post-surgical pain. The pathway offers targets for new painkillers.
plos-pone-0010991: New 2008 guidelines made far more HIV patients eligible for therapy. This study evaluates expanding HAART to all eligible adults in British Columbia. The paper models the epidemic impact. The finding supports earlier, broader treatment as sound public-health policy. The policy could turn the epidemic's tide.
plos-pone-0011091: The brain's stem cells receive conflicting orders. This study shows microglia-made interferon-gamma harms neural progenitors while the neuropeptide PACAP protects them. The paper reveals a survival tug-of-war. The finding informs brain-repair strategies. The tug-of-war decides the brain's regenerative fate.
plos-pone-0011191: The rarest Darwin's finch sings itself toward extinction. This study examines how sexual signals diverged in the rarest Galapagos finch — an evolutionary dead end. The paper reveals speciation gone awry. The finding informs conservation biology. The dead end warns conservationists.
plos-pone-0011291: A protein that helps cells swallow cargo has a built-in brake. This study defines the minimal autoinhibited unit of intersectin, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor. The paper reveals a self-regulation mechanism. The finding informs cell biology. The informed biology explains endocytosis control.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1291:
On 19 July 1945 the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. Someone had to think each question through on paper first; papers like this one are that thinking. The chiefs' staff supplied it in a steady flow through the talks.

A staff note from the third day belongs to the phase when stands were still soft. Facts and warnings could still move the envoys' minds. This memorandum carries the services' view at that open moment. It survives in the official record as part of the chiefs' near-daily counsel to the men who bargained for the United States.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1391:
Mikołajczyk's diary continues with an entry dated 29 July 1945. He was then in the middle of the Potsdam weeks, watching the settlement of Poland take shape around him. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

A diary kept day by day catches what later memoirs smooth away: rumor, waiting, and hope rising or falling on small news. This entry belongs to the summit's final stretch, when the leaders were drafting their closing texts. For readers, the value is closeness. The great questions of 1945 appear here at the scale of one man's day. Borders, armies, and governments fill a page written down before he knew how the story ended.
frus-1945-50-intel-d91:
Minutes of the eighth meeting of the Advisory Committee on Intelligence are dated 3 December 1946. The committee advised the State Department on its intelligence work. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A committee still meeting in December 1946 shows the State Department's intelligence function settling into a lasting, smaller form. The eighth meeting's minutes record routine where the autumn of 1945 had recorded upheaval. Readers can measure the change across the volume: from frantic memos about survival to numbered meetings about business. That settling is itself a result worth noting, the sound of a new order becoming normal inside an old department.
frus-1945-50-intel-d191:
The memorandum of 28 March 1947 is the work of the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence (Wright). In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 191, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d291:
On 17 June 1948, staff wrote up the discussion at the 13th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. Readers meet it as document 291 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time.

A memorandum of conversation is the note a participant or aide wrote after a talk, setting down who was there and what was said. For a reader, the gain is scene and voice, rare goods in a file of stiff forms. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d391:
A letter dated 29 July 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 391 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Reform talk filled the files that year, as the government weighed the Dulles team's harsh grades for the CIA.

A formal letter was a step above a memo: it put a request or a stance on record under the writer's signature. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1861-d91:
On 22 October 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams in his firm autumn tone. The letter is document 91 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Late October letters from Seward carry the feel of a man who has found his wartime stride. The orders are brief, the tone is firm, the goals are clear. This note to London shows the Secretary in full command of his far flung front. The orders assume Adams's full grasp, a trust the Secretary rarely gave so freely. Full command in the chief bred full effort in the man who served him.
frus-1861-d191:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Cassius Clay on 6 May 1861. Clay was the new American minister to Russia, bound for St. Petersburg. The letter is document 191 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Clay was a Kentucky emancipationist with a fighter's fame. Russia, under a young czar who had just freed the serfs, watched America with rare warmth. Seward's May letter sent Clay to the one great court that leaned toward the Union. Clay's fame as a duelist and emancipationist made him a marked man at any court. A marked man at court drew eyes, which Clay turned to the Union's gain.
frus-1861-d291:
Word from Mr. Harvey reached Washington on 28 July 1861, in a letter to William H. Seward. It stands as Document 291 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d91:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 5 July 1862. It stands as Document 91 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d191:
Document 191 is the second Seward dispatch to Charles Francis Adams dated 18 November 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams served as American minister in London, the post his father and grandfather had also held in earlier years.

Paired letters on one date often mean one carried the Secretary's orders while the other passed papers or news. The Adams legation answered in kind, and the printed file grows thick. For readers tracing how the Union kept Britain at arm's length in late 1862, the paired dispatches of November are core evidence. British backing for the South would have brought Richmond credit, ships, and fresh hope at once.
frus-1862-d291:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 23 June 1862 in a letter printed as Document 291 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Dayton wrote two days before the Seven Days battles began, in the last quiet of the Richmond campaign. French observers expected the capital's fall to settle the war's foreign side. His report belongs to that expectant week, and its value lies partly in its timing. It preserves what Paris believed just before events proved it wrong. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d391:
Document 391 is the second Seward dispatch to Simon Cameron dated 6 September 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward sent both letters to St. Petersburg together.

Same-day pairs on the Russian route mattered because sailings were rare; a missed mail could cost a month. Clerks therefore batched the post's business carefully. This second letter completes the September brief for St. Petersburg, and the pair together shows Washington briefing its Russian envoy on the invasion crisis as it began. Letters to Russia favored broad lines of policy over fast-changing battle news. The czar's government had freed its own serfs in 1861 and watched America's struggle closely.
frus-1862-d491:
On 2 April 1862 James Shepherd Pike sent this report from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 491 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Pike wrote days before the battle of Shiloh, in a lull when European opinion was weighing the war's cost against its likely end. The Dutch, careful neutrals with worldwide trade, wanted the fighting stopped but would not move first. His report measured that mood for Washington. Ministers' letters in this season also carried the small change of diplomacy: visits, dinners, and remarks that hinted at policy. Pike's blunt style makes his contributions to the volume unusually readable.
frus-1862-d591:
Dated 2 June 1862, this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Thomas Corwin was printed after the order of 7 June in the volume's Mexican file. It is Document 591 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The two June instructions, read together by date, show Seward handling the Mexican question in successive layers as reports from Corwin arrived. France's advance in Mexico posed the Union a problem it could not solve by force that year. So it solved it by record. The record held clear protests, kept promises of sympathy, and a paper trail for the future. Corwin's post was where that trail was laid. The letter is a working part of the longest-range policy in the whole volume.
frus-1862-d691: On 3 April 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to a Mr. De Long. The letter is document 691 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, answering the run of dispatches De Long had sent that winter. The evidence names both men and the date, but it does not state De Long's post or the letter's topic.
frus-1863p1-d91:
William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 25 February 1863, the second day in a row he wrote to London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 91 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Day-after-day letters from the secretary often chased a point that would not wait for the next steamer. For London, the points were steady ones: fair dealing from Britain, and a stop to warships for the South. This letter keeps that press on. It is a mid-run sheet, plain in form, whose weight comes from the chain of orders it belongs to.
frus-1863p1-d191:
Writing from London on 7 May 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 191 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

After the Emancipation Proclamation took effect on New Year's Day 1863, the war stood openly as a fight over slavery. That change made British support for the South harder to defend in public. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d291:
Washington's orders to London on 17 September 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 291 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Instructions like this one show how the Lincoln government ran a war abroad while fighting one at home. The paper trail is the diplomacy itself, order by order. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d391:
In Washington on 16 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 391 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons was the man Seward had to persuade, warn, or answer in person in Washington. Notes to him carried the American side of each dispute between the two governments. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d491:
The date 5 May 1863 heads a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d591:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 18 July 1863 letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d691:
Edwin M. Stanton, the Secretary of War, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 October 1863. The note is document 691 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863. Unlike most letters in this run, it comes from inside the Lincoln cabinet itself.

War and foreign affairs often met. Army and navy acts at sea or on the border could stir trouble with Britain at any time. Stanton's note brought the War Department's facts or views to the man who had to answer for them abroad. The reader sees the home side of diplomacy here. Before Seward spoke to foreign envoys, he needed word from his own team.
plos-pbio-0020091:
Mark J. Dayel and R. Dyche Mullins worked out a trigger step in cell shape change for PLOS Biology in 2004. Cells crawl and divide by building filaments of actin. The Arp2/3 complex starts new filaments branching off old ones, and WASP proteins switch it on.

The authors show how adding the first piece of a new filament, delivered by WASP, fires up the complex. That detail explains how the cell keeps actin growth off until the right place and moment. Precise timing matters, since wild actin growth would wreck cell shape. The mechanism is a neat case of a machine that arms itself with its own first building block.
plos-pbio-0020391:
Alekos Athanasiadis, Alexander Rich, and Stefan Maas surveyed RNA editing in human gene messages in PLOS Biology in 2004. Editing swaps one RNA letter for another after the message is made. The most common swap turns A into I, which the cell reads as G.

The team found this editing is far more widespread than thought, mostly in Alu repeats, which are common stretches in human messages. Widespread editing in repeats may help the cell mark and manage them. It also means the final protein code can differ from the DNA more often than assumed. The survey redrew the scale of editing and set off searches for its roles in brain function and disease.
plos-pone-0000091:
Paul de Groot and R. W. Veldhuizen described artery change in heart disease in PLOS ONE in 2006. Atherosclerosis is the buildup of fatty plaques inside arteries. As a plaque grows, the artery can widen outward to keep the channel open, a process called remodeling. Late in the disease, that compensation fails.

The authors trace remodeling from the start of plaque growth to its end stage in human coronary arteries. Seeing the whole arc in real tissue matters for treatment timing. Drugs and stents work on arteries at particular stages. A map of the full process helps doctors judge which stage a patient's artery has reached and what can still be saved.
plos-pone-0000191:
Chung-Ming Liu, Shu-Hua Lin, Ying-Chen Chen, and colleagues published this influenza study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines the timing of severe avian influenza A H5N1 outbreaks, the bird flu strain feared for its lethality. The authors link the onset of outbreaks to drops in temperature.

Cold snaps may change bird behavior, virus survival, or both, in ways that spark outbreaks. The authors test that link across outbreak records. If temperature drops really do precede flare-ups, weather data could give health and farm authorities a short warning window for a dangerous virus.
plos-pone-0000291:
Silvia Díaz, Francisco Amaro, Daniel Rico, and colleagues published this cell biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Metallothioneins are small proteins that bind metals, protecting cells from toxic ones like cadmium. In Tetrahymena, a single-celled pond organism, the authors show these proteins fall into two discrete subfamilies.

Two subfamilies suggest two distinct jobs, perhaps handling different metals or stresses. Sorting the family in this model organism clarifies how cells across life manage metal danger. Tetrahymena is a standard lab subject, so the classification guides work on pollution response and metal biology.
plos-pone-0000391:
Komla Sobo and colleagues looked inside the cell's recycling stations in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Late endosomes are compartments that sort material the cell has taken in, and their membranes contain raft-like domains, patches rich in certain fats. The team asked how varied those patches are.

Finding real diversity among the raft-like domains suggests the compartments are not uniform bags but have organized zones with different jobs. Membrane organization affects how cells sort cargo, break down waste, and respond to signals. Mapping that variety gives cell biologists a finer picture of a basic piece of cell machinery.
plos-pone-0000491:
Shobha Broor and colleagues followed young children in rural India for three years to map chest infections, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Acute respiratory infections are among the top killers of small children worldwide. The prospective cohort study tracked the epidemiology and virology of these infections, recording which viruses caused them and when.

A three-year window captures seasonal cycles and year-to-year variation that a short study would miss. Knowing the local virus mix guides vaccine and treatment priorities for the region. The study gives rural India, often absent from such data, a baseline that health planners can actually use.
plos-pone-0000591:
Jonathan Carlson and colleagues used the family-like layering of human groups to sharpen gene hunts, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Gene hunts link DNA variants to disease. They are plagued by false hits when the groups being compared differ in ancestry. The team showed how to use layered population structure to clean up such studies.

Human groups nest inside each other: broad regions hold local groups, which hold smaller ones still. Using that layering lets the math split true disease links from mere ancestry gaps. Cleaner methods mean fewer wasted years chasing phantom genes. That was a real cost in the first wave of genome-wide scans.
plos-pone-0000691:
Andre Franke, Jochen Hampe, Philip Rosenstiel and colleagues used systematic association mapping to name a new disease gene, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Crohn disease is one form of inflammatory bowel disease, driven by many genes together. Recent studies had found several Crohn-linked variants. Together they explained only a fraction of the disease's heritability, so more genes remained hidden.

Their mapping identified NELL1 as a novel IBD disease gene. Each new susceptibility gene adds a piece to the inherited puzzle and a possible drug target. Systematic scans like this one replaced guesswork candidate-gene studies, and NELL1 is presented as a catch from casting the net widely.
plos-pone-0000791:
Christian B. Willberg, Scott M. Ward, Reginald F. Clayton and colleagues found that an immune signal can shield liver cells from immune attack. Cellular immunity plays a key role in the outcome of hepatitis C virus infection, yet most infections become persistent. The mechanisms behind that persistence were unclear, but the liver, the primary site of infection, may be critical, as their 2007 PLOS ONE study argues.

The title states the finding: interferon-alpha protects hepatocytes, liver cells, from killing by cytotoxic T cells. A signal meant to fight virus may also preserve infected cells, balancing damage against control. That trade-off could help explain why hepatitis C so often settles in for the long term.
plos-pone-0000891:
Ingo Meister and Marco Iacoboni asked whether language areas switch on when people watch actions with meaning, in PLOS ONE in 2007. One idea holds that language grew out of brain systems for movement. Front and side brain areas that react to watched actions are part of that story.

If language truly grew from those systems, watching an action with a clear message might wake language areas too. The authors tested that expectation and report no language specific activation in their setup. A negative result like this is useful: it sets limits on a popular theory. It pushes the field to say more exactly which systems language and action really share.
plos-pone-0000991:
Mark Tarnopolsky, Andrew Zimmer, Jeremy Paikin and colleagues tested two supplements with strength training in older adults, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Aging brings lower muscle mass and more body fat. The team asked whether creatine monohydrate and conjugated linoleic acid could add to the gains from resistance exercise.

Older volunteers trained while taking the supplements, and the team tracked strength and body composition, including fat free mass and body fat. Supplements are widely sold to this age group on thin evidence. A controlled trial in the exact population that buys them is the right test. The paper reports what the combination did and did not add.
plos-pone-0001091:
Anil Thakur, Gautier Robin, Gregor Guncar and colleagues improved protein crystallization screening with seed particles, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Growing crystals is a major bottleneck in reading protein structures by X-ray methods. A crystal must first nucleate, start from a seed, then grow to usable size, and that start is often the failure point.

Adding heterogeneous nucleating agents, foreign particles that invite nucleation, raised success in sparse matrix screening, the standard first pass test. A better first pass saves protein, time and money on every structure project. Structural biology feeds drug design, so a bench trick that lifts success rates has wide downstream value.
plos-pone-0001191:
Can a simple body tissue detect an image, the way an eye does? Catherine Tempel-Brami, Iddo Pinkas, and Avigdor Scherz explored that odd question in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They used a living rat and a pigment injected into the bloodstream.

Light absorbed through the body was translated by the tissue into a chemical signature, which the authors visualized using photosensitized magnetic resonance imaging. In effect, the tissue itself acted as the light sensor and the scanner read the picture. The study is a proof of principle for imaging methods that borrow the body's own chemistry.
plos-pone-0001291:
Many bacterial pathogens inject proteins into host cells using a type III secretion system, a molecular syringe. Lian Zhou, Jing Wang, and Lian-Hui Zhang found a control circuit for that syringe in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Screening a mutant library, they found that breaking the genes for a spermidine transporter changed secretion.

The authors describe modulation of the type III secretion system by a spermidine transporter dependent signaling pathway. Spermidine is a small molecule cells use in many processes. Linking its transport to the injection machinery reveals a new place where a pathogen's attack could be blocked.
plos-pone-0001391:
Hyun-Gwan Lee and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on alcohol and mating acts in fruit flies. In people, drinking is tied to bold and loose mating behavior. Hard proof for the body basis of that link was thin. The team sought a lab model where the link could be tested in a strict way.

They gave male flies repeat doses of alcohol vapor and watched their courtship of females. The males grew bold and kept courting even when it made little sense. A fly model like this lets labs probe the genes and brain paths at play. That may in time clarify how drink loosens restraint in people too.
plos-pone-0001491:
Ling Li and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on herpes virus infection in the cell nucleus. A helper protein called Hsc70 gathers in spots inside infected nuclei. Parts of the cell's waste system gather there too. The team had shown the virus's gene copying sites sit in those spots. They asked what viral part calls Hsc70 there.

They show a viral protein called ICP27 is needed for Hsc70 to form its spots. Those spots sit at the edge of the virus's copying zones. The finding ties a host helper to a key viral worker. Blocking that tie could be a route to curb herpes growth.
plos-pone-0001591:
Marc Mangel and Michael Bonsall published a 2008 PLOS ONE paper that brings evolution models to stem cell science. Such models have served well in much of biology, but had not been used for stem cells save for cancer work. The pair build a frame that lets these models run on stem cells in full. It covers cell replacement, rest states, and variation.

With the frame, labs can test how stem cell pools hold up over a life span. They can also test how faults grow into disease in a formal way. Math frames like this turn loose tales into claims that data can check. That is a gain for a fast, hype prone field.
plos-pone-0001691:

baxter-certainty-of-the-worlds-of-spirit:
Richard Baxter, the leading Puritan divine of his age, published The Certainty of the Worlds of Spirits in 1691. Skepticism about spirits was rising in England, and Baxter meant to crush it with evidence. He marshals case after case of apparitions and witchcraft, each offered as proved fact.

Baxter argues that doubting spirits leads straight to doubting God. His stories come with names, places, and sworn witnesses. The book is the heavyweight anti-skeptic tract of the 1690s, earnest and formidable. Readers can watch a great preacher turn detective for the invisible world. Its pile of cases still impresses, whatever a reader concludes.
bekker-betoverde-weereld-dutch-1691:
Balthasar Bekker, a Dutch minister, published De betoverde weereld, The World Bewitched, in 1691. Across four books he attacks the belief that demons act directly on the physical world. His argument is the most radical skeptical stroke of the early Enlightenment, and it cost him his pulpit.

Bekker reads Scripture closely and finds no warrant for the reigning devil lore. Devils, he holds, cannot move bodies, raise storms, or possess the mad. The church that tried him proved how dangerous such reason seemed. His book spread across Europe in many tongues. It marks the moment when demonology began its long retreat in learned Europe.
binsfeld-tractatus-confessionibus-latin-:
Peter Binsfeld, suffragan bishop of Trier, published his treatise on the confessions of witches in 1591. Latin gave the work its learned reach. Trier then stood near the peak of the great German witch persecution, and Binsfeld helped shape its course from within the church.

His question sounds careful: how much faith should courts place in witches' confessions? His answers, though, armed the prosecutors. Confessions gained under torture could name new suspects, and Binsfeld's rules let the hunt widen. The book became the leading Catholic demonology of the persecution's height. It shows law and theology harnessed together to the burning times.
grillandi-tractatus-de-sortilegiis-latin:
Paolo Grillandi, an Italian judge who served the papal court, wrote his treatise on sorcery in the earlier sixteenth century. It circulated here in the Frankfurt Tractatus duo of 1591, a standard gathering of witchcraft law. Grillandi writes from the bench, and his Latin sets out inquisitorial demonology at its most systematic.

He defines sorcery, divides its kinds, and lays down how courts should prove it. Confession, witnesses, and signs each get their rules. The treatise taught judges across Italy and beyond how to run a witch trial. Law for the witch courts is here written by a judge who knew them from inside. Its system is the point, and the terror, of the book.
ponzinibio-de-lamiis-latin-1591:
Gianfrancesco Ponzinibio, a jurist of Piacenza, wrote De lamiis, on witches, early in the sixteenth century. This text comes from the Frankfurt Tractatus duo of 1591, which revived his daring argument. Ponzinibio holds that the witches' flight and sabbath are illusions, not bodily events.

As a lawyer, he attacks the evidence itself. Dreams and torture, he argues, cannot build a capital case. His tract is the daring precursor that Johann Weyer later built upon. Skeptics across Europe cited Ponzinibio as their early authority. The book's courage is plain: a working jurist told the witch courts, in Latin, that their central scene never happened.
